sections.b: Jacob's name is explained from 'aqev, "heel" (25:26), and Esau turns it into a verb, ya'qeveni: "He has grabbed me by the heel these two times" (27:36). He takes the birthright and, with his mother's plan and his father's blindness, the blessing (ch. 27). Fleeing, he meets God at Bethel (28:10–22). In Haran the deceiver is deceived: Laban gives him Leah in place of Rachel (29:25), and twenty years of labor follow (31:38–41). Coming home, he wrestles a man until dawn at the Jabbok, is lamed, and is renamed Israel, "for you have struggled with God and with humans and have won" (32:28). He is reconciled with Esau (ch. 33), but is silent while Dinah is violated and angry mainly about his own danger after his sons' massacre (34:5, 30). God sends him back to Bethel, confirms the name, and the chapter of his life closes with Rachel's death and Isaac's burial (ch. 35).

sections.b: Jewish tradition mostly honors Jacob as the "quiet man who stayed among the tents" (25:27), in tradition the "perfect" (tam) man, the Torah scholar of the house of Shem and Eber (Rashi on 25:27; Genesis Rabbah 63:10), whose deceptions were forced on him by his mother's prophecy. Yet the rabbis also note that he paid for every trick: tricked by Laban with a sister, by his sons with a goat and a robe (37:31). Christian readers have often seen him as proof that grace chooses the unworthy (Romans 9:11–13), and Luther and Calvin both defend and criticize him. Modern literary readers (Robert Alter, J. P. Fokkelman) see a man slowly remade by measure-for-measure suffering.
sections.refs: Genesis 25:27; Genesis 27:19; Genesis 29:25–26; Genesis 37:31–33; Hosea 12:2–6; Romans 9:11–13

common: Jacob is often pictured as a pure villain or a pure hero. Genesis presents both sides without resolving them: God's promise stands, and Jacob still reaps what he sows.

claude.title: The two blessing scenes mirror each other
claude.body: J. P. Fokkelman, Nahum Sarna and Robert Alter all note the contrast between "It is I, Esau" (27:19) and "Jacob" (32:27). Claude adds a small point: both scenes turn on a question about who he is, "Who are you, my son?" (27:18) and "What is your name?" (32:27). The first time, Jacob answers with a lie and gets a blessing he must run away from; the second time he answers truthfully and gets a blessing that lets him go home.

sections.b: Esau marries two Hittite women, a grief to his parents (26:34–35), loses the blessing and weeps aloud (27:34–38), and plans to kill his brother once Isaac dies (27:41). Twenty years later he comes with four hundred men, but runs to Jacob, embraces him and weeps (33:4), and refuses his gift at first: "I have plenty, my brother" (33:9). Genesis 36 lists his descendants, the chiefs of Edom and the Horite clans of Seir, and the kings who "reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel" (36:31). The double word-play runs through: Esau is "red" ('admoni, 25:25), asks for the "red stuff" (25:30), and lives in Seir, which sounds like se'ar, "hair" (27:11).

sections.h: Edom as Rome in Jewish tradition
sections.b: From about the second century AD the rabbis read "Edom" and "Esau" as code for Rome, and later for Christian Europe. Isaac's words "the voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are Esau's hands" (27:22) were applied to Hadrian's destruction of Jewish communities (Gittin 57b; Lamentations Rabbah). Esau's kiss (33:4), marked with dots in the Hebrew text, prompted the debate whether he kissed sincerely or tried to bite (Genesis Rabbah 78:9). Maimonides and others still wrote of Christian powers as "Edom."

Egyptian records mention Shasu of Seir and of Edom in the 13th and 12th centuries BC. Excavations at Bozrah (Buseirah) found a capital of the 8th–6th centuries, which led many scholars to doubt a kingdom of Edom before David (36:31). Copper mining at Khirbat en-Nahas, dated by radiocarbon to the 11th–10th centuries BC (Levy et al.), has reopened the question of an early Edomite state.

uncommon: The list of Edomite kings who reigned "before any king reigned over the people of Israel" (36:31) is one that Spinoza argued could not have been written before Israel had kings. Ibn Ezra, whose hints at later additions elsewhere (12:6; Deuteronomy 1:2) Spinoza drew on, rejected a late date for this verse.

sections.b: Jacob meets Rachel at the well and weeps (29:11), serves seven years that seem to him "a few days" (29:20), and is tricked into marrying Leah first. Rachel is loved but childless, and cries to Jacob, "Give me children! If you don't, I am a dead woman" (30:1). She gives her slave Bilhah, bargains for Leah's mandrakes (30:14–15), and at last bears Joseph, "May the LORD add another son for me" (30:24). She steals her father's household gods and hides them by sitting on them, pleading her period (31:19, 34–35). Her own words "I am a dead woman" come true when she dies giving birth to Benjamin, naming him Ben-oni (35:16–20), "son of my sorrow."

Jacob set a pillar on her grave "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (35:19–20). Jeremiah hears "Rachel weeping for her children" at Ramah as the exiles are led away (Jeremiah 31:15), and Matthew applies it to Herod's killing of Bethlehem's children (Matthew 2:18). A midrash says Jacob buried her by the road so she could pray for her exiled descendants (Genesis Rabbah 82:10; Rashi on 48:7). Two traditions place her tomb: near Bethlehem, where the shrine stands today, and in Benjamin's territory near Ramah (1 Samuel 10:2).

common: Rachel is often remembered as only the beautiful favorite. The text also gives her anger, cunning, grief and an early death.

sections.b: Leah's "eyes were soft" (29:17), rakkot, either weak or delicate, and the word has been read both ways for two thousand years. Laban brings her to Jacob in the dark (29:23). When God sees that she is "hated" (Hebrew senu'ah, the legal term for the less-loved wife, Deuteronomy 21:15), he opens her womb (29:31). Her sons' names trace her hope: Reuben, "the LORD has seen my misery"; Simeon, "the LORD heard"; Levi, "now my husband will join himself to me"; then Judah: "This time I will praise the LORD" (29:32–35). From Levi came Israel's priests, from Judah its kings and, Christians add, the Messiah (Matthew 1:2–3). The elders of Bethlehem bless Ruth to be "like Rachel and Leah, the two who built the house of Israel" (Ruth 4:11).

uncommon: The rabbis said Leah's eyes were weak from weeping, because people said the elder daughter was meant for Esau the elder son (Bava Batra 123a; Genesis Rabbah 70:16).

sections.b: Laban welcomes Jacob as "my bone and my flesh" (29:14), then uses him as hired labor. He swaps Leah for Rachel (29:23–26) and changes Jacob's wages "ten times" (31:7, 41). Jacob outbreeds him with peeled rods (30:37–43), and flees. Laban chases him seven days, searches for his stolen gods and finds nothing (31:33–35). The two make a covenant with a stone heap, called Jegar-sahadutha in Aramaic and Galeed in Hebrew (31:47), both meaning "heap of witness," and agree that neither will cross it to harm the other. Laban kisses his daughters and grandchildren and goes home (31:55). The Passover Haggadah, commenting on Deuteronomy 26:5, reads it as "an Aramean tried to destroy my father," and says Laban sought to uproot everything.

Genesis 26 is the only chapter that centers on Isaac as an adult. Facing famine, he is told not to go to Egypt, receives the promise sworn to Abraham "because Abraham listened to my voice" (26:2–5), passes Rebekah off as his sister at Gerar (26:7), prospers a hundredfold (26:12), and reopens his father's wells until the Philistines stop quarreling (26:18–22). Abimelech seeks a treaty with him at Beersheba (26:26–31). Old and blind, Isaac means to bless Esau and is deceived into blessing Jacob, then shakes "with a great trembling, past all measure" when he learns of it (27:33). He sends Jacob off with the blessing of Abraham (28:1–4), and dies at 180 years, buried by both sons (35:28–29). God is later called "the Fear of Isaac" (31:42, 53).
sections.refs: Genesis 26:1–35; Genesis 27:1–40; Genesis 28:1–4; Genesis 31:42; Genesis 35:27–29; Hebrews 11:20

uncommon: Isaac's age at his death (180) means, by Genesis's own numbers, that he lived on for about twelve years after Joseph was sold. The story tells his death early, out of order, to finish with him before Joseph's story begins; the rabbis' rule "there is no earlier or later in the Torah" (Pesachim 6b) covers such cases.

sections.b: Jacob reaches "the place" (28:11), sleeps with a stone at his head, and dreams of a stairway with angels and the LORD standing beside or above it. He wakes saying "The LORD really is in this place, and I did not know it" and "This is nothing but the house of God, and this is heaven's gate" (28:16–17). He sets up the stone as a pillar, anoints it, renames Luz Bethel, and vows a tenth (28:18–22). Twenty years later God reminds him of the vow (31:13). After Shechem he commands his household to bury their foreign gods and goes back to Bethel to build an altar, El-bethel (35:1–7). There Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, is buried under the "oak of weeping" (35:8), and God renews the name Israel and the promise (35:9–15).

Bethel is usually identified with Beitin, about 12 miles north of Jerusalem, though some scholars prefer nearby el-Bireh. Critical scholars think the Jacob-at-Bethel stories may have supported the Bethel shrine of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29), and that the phrase "house of God" set it up as a rival claim to Jerusalem's temple. Traditional scholars reply that an old patriarchal holy place is exactly why Jeroboam chose Bethel. Excavations at Beitin in the 1930s and 1950s (Albright, Kelso) reported Bronze and Iron Age remains, but the dating has been disputed (Finkelstein and Singer-Avitz).

The Hebrew sullam appears only here (28:12). It is probably related to Akkadian simmiltu, "stairway," and many scholars think of the great staircases of Mesopotamian temple-towers, where gods were thought to come down. The angels go up first and then come down. Rashi says the angels of the land of Israel went up and the angels of exile came down to escort Jacob. Another midrash says the angels went up and down "on him" (Hebrew bo can mean "on it" or "on him"), comparing Jacob's face on earth with his image in heaven (Genesis Rabbah 68:12). Jesus seems to use the same reading: the angels ascend and descend "on the Son of Man" (John 1:51). For Christians, Jesus is the true Bethel and gate of heaven. The image became a common symbol of spiritual ascent, as in John Climacus's Ladder of Divine Ascent.

common: The word is usually translated "ladder," but a stairway or ramp fits the Hebrew and the ancient world better.

sections.b: Esau sells his birthright (bekhorah) for a bowl of stew (25:29–34), and Jacob takes his blessing (berakhah) by deceit (ch. 27). The two words sound alike, and Esau makes the pun himself: "He took my birthright, and look, now he has taken my blessing" (27:36). Isaac's blessing could not be taken back: "I blessed him. Yes, and blessed he will be" (27:33). Many readers see a spoken blessing as working like a will or a binding oath in the ancient world. The second blessing Isaac gives Esau is almost the reverse of Jacob's: "away from the richness of the earth" (27:39). Jacob later demands a blessing from the man at the Jabbok (32:26), and tries to give a "blessing" (a gift, 33:11) back to Esau. Hebrews 12:16–17 warns readers not to be like Esau, who "in exchange for one meal ... sold his own birthright" and found no way to change his father's mind, though he looked for it with tears.

claude.title: Returning the stolen blessing
claude.body: Jacob's "Please take my blessing" (33:11) can be read as returning, in a gift of flocks, the blessing he stole in ch. 27; Fokkelman and others note this. Claude adds that Esau's acceptance, after first refusing (33:9), is what lets the story move on: the gift only works as a return when the wronged brother agrees to take it.

sections.h: Jacob I loved, Esau I hated
sections.b: Before the twins are born, Rebekah hears, "the elder will serve the younger" (25:23). Malachi recalls it: "Jacob I loved. But Esau I hated" (Malachi 1:2–3), speaking of the two nations. Paul quotes both texts to show that God's choosing comes "not by works but by the one who calls" (Romans 9:11–13). In Hebrew idiom "hate" can mean "love less" or "not choose" (compare 29:30–31 of Leah, and Luke 14:26). Interpreters still argue whether Paul means individuals destined to salvation (Augustine, Calvin), or nations and their place in God's plan (many Arminian, Catholic and New Perspective readers). Jewish readers note that Esau too is blessed and given his land (Deuteronomy 2:5).
sections.refs: Genesis 25:23; Genesis 27:29; Genesis 27:40; Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:10–13; Deuteronomy 2:5; Luke 14:26

sections.b: God confirms to Isaac "the oath that I swore to Abraham" (26:3) and repeats the promise to Jacob at Bethel (28:13–15) and again on his return (35:11–12). Two human treaties follow the ancient pattern of oath, witness and shared meal. Abimelech asks Isaac for an oath (alah) and covenant (26:28–31), and the two "swore, each man to his brother," after a feast, which explains the name Shibah, "oath" or "seven," at Beersheba (26:33). Jacob and Laban set a stone pillar and heap, call God to watch between them, eat together on the heap and swear (31:44–54). Ancient Near Eastern treaties from Mari and Hatti also set boundary stones and call gods as witnesses.

In Genesis 34, Jacob's sons answer Shechem's request "with trickery" (34:13): they will intermarry if every male in the city is circumcised, since "that would be a disgrace for us" (34:14). On the third day, "while they were in pain," Simeon and Levi kill them all (34:25). The sign of God's covenant (17:10–14) becomes the means of revenge. Jacob curses their anger on his deathbed (49:5–7). Some later readers, such as the book of Jubilees (ch. 30), praised the brothers for zeal against intermarriage; others, ancient and modern, have seen the episode as a warning against using sacred signs for violence.

Dinah "went out to look at the daughters of the land" (34:1). Shechem son of Hamor "took her and lay with her and dishonored her" (34:2). The verb 'innah means to humble or abuse, and in sexual contexts usually means rape (compare 2 Samuel 13:14). Then "His soul clung to Dinah" he loved her and "spoke to the girl's heart" (34:3), and asked his father to get her for him as a wife. Her brothers call it "a disgraceful thing in Israel" (34:7) and ask, "Like a prostitute, is that how he should treat our sister?" (34:31). A minority of scholars (Lyn Bechtel, Ellen van Wolde) argue the text describes an unauthorized marriage rather than force, but most read it as rape. Dinah never speaks, and we do not hear what she wanted.

Some rabbis blamed Dinah for "going out" (Genesis Rabbah 80:1), a reading many modern Jewish and Christian readers reject. Others gave her a future: Simeon promised to marry her (Genesis Rabbah 80:11); she married Job (Bava Batra 15b; Genesis Rabbah 57:4), or her daughter by Shechem was Asenath, who later married Joseph (Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer 38; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on 41:45). Anita Diamant's novel The Red Tent (1997) retold the story from Dinah's point of view.

common: Some sermons treat 34:1 as a warning to young women not to go out alone. The text itself places the blame on Shechem's act (34:2, 7) and on the violence of her brothers.

sections.b: Genesis 34 uses three verbs, "took... lay with... violated" (34:2), the same sequence used of Amnon and Tamar (2 Samuel 13:14). The narrator calls it "a disgraceful thing in Israel... such a thing is not done" (34:7). Then the story moves to the men: Hamor bargains, Jacob is silent, and the brothers plan deceit. Shechem keeps Dinah in his house (34:26). Simeon and Levi's revenge kills every male in the city and their brothers plunder it, taking the women and children captive (34:25–29), so that the answer to one woman's violation is the capture of many others. Jacob's rebuke is about his own danger (34:30); his sons' last word is about their sister (34:31). The chapter leaves the reader with the question it does not answer.

Jacob arrives "safely" (or "at Shalem") at the city of Shechem, buys a plot of land for a hundred qesitah from the sons of Hamor, and builds an altar he names El-Elohe-Israel (33:18–20), "God, the God of Israel." Joseph is later buried in this field (Joshua 24:32), and John's Gospel places Jacob's well nearby (John 4:5–6). The city's prince, also named Shechem, violates Dinah, and her brothers destroy the town (ch. 34). Before leaving for Bethel, Jacob buries the foreign gods "under the oak that is by Shechem" (35:4). Excavations at Tell Balata found a large Middle Bronze Age city with massive walls and a fortress-temple, and Shechem appears in the Amarna letters (14th century BC) as the base of the ruler Labayu.

Jacob sets up four stones in Genesis 28–35: the stone at his head at Bethel, anointed with oil (28:18, 22); the pillar and heap of witness with Laban (31:45–52); a second pillar at Bethel with a drink offering (35:14); and the pillar over Rachel's grave, standing "to this day" (35:20). Each one marks a meeting with God, a treaty or a death. Later law forbade setting up such pillars (Deuteronomy 16:22). Jewish commentators explained the difference: Rashi, following the Sifre, said a pillar was loved in the patriarchs' day but hated once the Canaanites made it a rite of their idols (Rashi on Deuteronomy 16:22).

Rachel steals her father's teraphim as Jacob flees (31:19). Laban calls them "my gods" (31:30). She hides them in a camel saddle and sits on them, telling her father, "the way of women is upon me" (31:34–35). Why she took them is not said. Rashi says she wanted to turn her father from idolatry; Ibn Ezra, that she feared Laban would use them to divine where Jacob had gone. A once-popular theory, based on a tablet from Nuzi, held that owning household gods gave a claim to the family inheritance; later study of the Nuzi texts (Moshe Greenberg and others) has made that much less certain. Later, Jacob tells his household to put away their "foreign gods" and buries them at Shechem (35:2–4). The narrator's mockery is clear: household gods can be sat on by a woman in her period.

Jacob vows at Bethel: if God will be with him, give him bread and clothes and bring him home in peace, then "the LORD will be my God," the stone will be God's house, "and of everything you give me I will give a tenth, a tenth to you" (28:20–22). The Hebrew doubles the verb, "tithing I will tithe." The text never says how or when the vow was paid. Some readers think the return to Bethel in 35:1–15 is its fulfillment, and critics think the verse explains the tithe brought to the royal shrine at Bethel (Amos 4:4).

Jacob's household shows the price of polygamy more clearly than anywhere else in the Bible. He loves Rachel more than Leah (29:30), and God sees that Leah is "hated" (29:31). The sisters compete through their sons' names (29:32–30:24), each giving her slave woman, Bilhah and Zilpah, to Jacob as a surrogate (30:3–13). Rachel names Naphtali "my wrestling": "I have wrestled God's wrestlings with my sister, and I have won" (30:8). The later law that a man must not marry his wife's sister as a rival while she lives (Leviticus 18:18) reads like a judgment on this story. The rivalry passes to the sons: Reuben lies with Bilhah (35:22), and Rachel's son Joseph is hated by Leah's sons (ch. 37).

Genesis 36:12 says Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz son of Esau, and she bore him Amalek. Amalek is also listed among the "chiefs" of Eliphaz (36:16). The rabbis asked why Timna, a Horite princess (36:22), would accept being a concubine, and said she wanted so much to join Abraham's family that she said, "Let me be a concubine to this nation rather than a princess of another" (Sanhedrin 99b). They concluded that Israel should not have rejected her, and Amalek was the result. Genesis 14:7 mentions "the whole country of the Amalekites" before Esau was born, which ancient readers explained as using a later name.

sections.b: Jacob meets angels at both ends of his journey. Leaving the land, he sees "angels of God going up and going down" at Bethel (28:12). Returning, "angels of God met him," and he names the place Mahanaim, "two camps" (32:1–2). That night he sends "messengers" to Esau, the same Hebrew word mal'akhim (32:3). At the Jabbok "a man" wrestles with him (32:24), whom Jacob says was God (32:30) and whom Hosea calls an angel (Hosea 12:4). Jewish tradition named him Esau's guardian angel (Genesis Rabbah 77:3); many Christian fathers saw in him the pre-incarnate Word.

Genesis 26–36 adds several names. God is "the God of Abraham your father" to Isaac (26:24), and "the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac" to Jacob (31:42). Albrecht Alt argued that "Fear of Isaac" (pachad Yitzchaq) was the old name of a clan god, and some prefer "Kinsman of Isaac." "El Shaddai" blesses Jacob (28:3; 35:11). Jacob names an altar El-Elohe-Israel (33:20) and a place El-bethel (35:7). Peniel means "face of God" (32:30). Laban swears by "the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor" (31:53).

sections.b: Eleven of Jacob's twelve sons are born in Haran (29:31–30:24), and Benjamin in the land, on the road to Bethlehem (35:16–18). Each name is explained by a pun in his mother's mouth. Genesis 35:23–26 lists them by mother: Leah's six (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun), Rachel's two (Joseph, Benjamin), Bilhah's two (Dan, Naphtali) and Zilpah's two (Gad, Asher). Many critical scholars think the list reflects the later grouping of tribes, with the "slave" tribes on the edges of Israel's land.

Genesis 36 is the longest genealogy of a non-chosen line in the Bible. It follows the pattern of Genesis: the rejected line is listed first and briefly (Ishmael in 25:12–18, Esau here), before the story returns to the chosen line (37:2). Its lists include Esau's wives and sons, the chiefs ('allufim), the Horite clans of Seir, and eight kings of Edom, none succeeding his father. Its names differ in places from 1 Chronicles 1:35–54 and from Esau's wives in 26:34 and 28:9.

Isaac lives as a sojourner in Gerar, and Abimelech the Philistine is more upright than he is: he rebukes Isaac for the sister lie (26:10), protects Rebekah, and later seeks a treaty, saying, "We have seen with our own eyes that the LORD has been with you" (26:28). Philistines in the patriarchal period are often called an anachronism, since the Philistines arrived about 1175 BC; some conservative scholars (Kenneth Kitchen) suggest an earlier Aegean group with the same name.

sections.h: Rachel's grave on the road to Bethlehem
sections.b: Rachel dies "some distance" from Ephrath and is buried "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (35:16–19). Ephrath(ah) is the clan name linked to Bethlehem in Ruth 4:11 and Micah 5:2. Whether the gloss "which is Bethlehem" is original or an early scribal note, and whether Rachel's grave was nearer Bethlehem or Ramah (1 Samuel 10:2; Jeremiah 31:15), is debated.

On the night before he meets Esau, Jacob prays, "I am too small for all the faithful love and all the faithfulness you have shown your servant. With only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps" (32:10). It is the first prayer of thanks in his life and admits he has earned nothing. Christians often read the whole Jacob story as grace shown to the unworthy (Romans 9:11–16).

Jacob's prayer at the Jabbok uses the plural chasadim, "acts of faithful love" (the Plain English Translation has "all the faithful love"), with "faithfulness" ('emet, 32:10), the pair later used in God's self-description at Sinai, "great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). The same pair describes God's kindness to Abraham's servant at the well (24:27), which brought Rebekah to Isaac. Jacob, who has deceived his father and uncle, now admits that God has kept faith with him without fail. Later, the dying Jacob asks Joseph to "deal with me in faithful love and truth" by burying him in Canaan (47:29).
